(CNN) -- Efraim Diveroli's father had once hoped his son would pursue a career as a doctor or lawyer. Instead, at just 22 years old, Diveroli has become an international arms dealer now facing a congressional inquiry over allegations that his company sold aging Chinese ammunition to the U.S. military for use by allies in Afghanistan.

Diveroli serves as president of AEY Inc., a South Florida-based company that, according to U.S. government documents, has conducted more than $10 million in business with the U.S. government since 2004. These records also reveal that the company achieved a major breakthrough in 2007, securing contracts exceeding $200 million to supply ammunition, assault rifles, and other weaponry to the Afghan National Army and police forces.

Although the company's contract specified that the ammunition would be sourced from Hungary, Army investigators discovered that the Afghan military had instead received corroded ammunition manufactured in China as far back as 46 years ago. The New York Times reported Thursday that AEY had sourced weapons from stockpiles and ammunition depots across former Soviet bloc nations, ranging from Albania to Kazakhstan. According to the Times, Albania had been a major purchaser of Chinese armaments during the 1960s and '70s.

Angelo Diveroli, Efraim's grandfather, told CNN affiliate WPLG-TV that his grandson is being unfairly targeted by "jealous competitors" within the international arms market. The elder Diveroli explained that Efraim has demonstrated an aptitude for weapons since childhood.

"He's a genius about anything to do with weapons," the 72-year-old said. "Ever since he was a little boy, I would take him to gun shows and he could identify every model of gun. People would ask: How can he do that so young? He has a gift, I would tell them."

Michael Diveroli, Efraim's father, told CNN affiliate WFOR-TV that he wished his son had directed his considerable intellect toward a different path. He described Efraim as "a boy genius" who is "hard to control."

"I would prefer he became a nice Jewish doctor or lawyer rather than an arms dealer," WFOR quoted Michael Diveroli as saying.

Yet his son appeared to possess a clear understanding of the circles in which he operated. "What goes on in the Albanian Defense Ministry," the New York Times quoted him as saying. "Who's clean? Who's dirty? Don't want to know about it."

On a MySpace page last updated in 2005, Efraim Diveroli wrote that he had "probably grew up way to (sic) fast." Yet even then, at 19, he hinted at the trajectory his future would take: "I definately (sic) have the desire to be very successful in my business and this does take up alot (sic) of my time."

The page also revealed a penchant for excitement. "I'm one of those guys who needs to be entertained and having lots of fun all the time so if your (sic) also an undiagnosed case of ADD look me up," he wrote, listing the weapon-centric films "Heat" and "Scarface" among his favorites.

A CNN review of Diveroli's Florida criminal record reveals several arrests—though no convictions—on charges ranging from misdemeanor battery to felony possession of stolen property. He has yet to appear in court following a March 3 arrest for driving under the influence.

According to relatives, Efraim Diveroli is currently out of the country, and CNN's attempts to reach him have been unsuccessful. His grandfather told WPLG that Diveroli is presently in either Turkey or Albania, fulfilling what he described as his "patriotic" duty.

"He's all over the world getting what the military needs," Angelo Diveroli said.

However, in a MySpace exchange with Radar magazine, a person believed to be David Packouz—the 25-year-old former vice president of AEY—referred to Efraim Diveroli as his "former scumbag partner," suggesting that Diveroli's primary motivation is financial gain. "Efraim Diveroli has a serious psychological illness called 'extreme greed,'" Radar quoted him as writing in a report published on its website.

When contacted by CNN on Friday, Packouz declined to discuss AEY, citing the ongoing investigation.

**MIAMI, FL** — The story of Efraim Diveroli reads like a Hollywood script—which, fittingly, it eventually became. The Miami Beach native's journey from a 21-year-old arms dealer to federal convict has raised serious questions about oversight in U.S. military contracting.

In 2007, AEY Inc. secured a contract worth nearly $300 million from the U.S. Army to supply ammunition to Afghan security forces. The scandal erupted when investigative journalists and military officials discovered that a significant portion of the ammunition being shipped was:

- **Decades-old Chinese-manufactured munitions**, violating U.S. arms embargo laws
- **Repackaged to disguise its origin**, with workers allegedly instructed to remove original packaging
- **Of questionable reliability**, raising concerns for soldiers depending on functional equipment in combat zones

His young age at the time of the offenses—barely old enough to legally purchase alcohol when he began brokering international arms deals—became a focal point of public fascination.

### Cultural Aftermath

The scandal later inspired the 2016 film *War Dogs*, starring Miles Teller as a character based on Diveroli's business partner, with Jonah Hill playing a character modeled after Diveroli himself. The film brought renewed attention to the case, dramatizing how young, inexperienced brokers exploited loopholes in federal contracting systems meant to encourage competitive bidding.

The company in question won its massive contract through a competitive bidding process, undercutting established competitors on price. For a moment, it looked like a triumph of entrepreneurial hustle over bureaucratic inertia.

Then journalists and investigators began asking harder questions.

## The Scrutiny Intensifies

What followed was a familiar pattern in procurement scandals: a scramble by government agencies to explain how safeguards had failed, testimony before skeptical lawmakers, and a young executive facing consequences that seemed to outpace his professional experience.

## The Lasting Questions

What remains most striking about cases like this isn't simply the individual's culpability—it's what the episode reveals about systemic vulnerabilities. When speed and cost dominate procurement decisions, especially in wartime, the incentives can align poorly with rigorous oversight.

The ammunition that flows to soldiers in combat zones isn't an abstraction; equipment failures or fraudulent sourcing carry consequences beyond financial loss. As governments continue outsourcing complex logistics to private contractors, the central tension endures: how to maintain the agility that smaller firms offer without sacrificing the safeguards that larger, more established contractors are presumed—rightly or wrongly—to provide.
